**Yoga Sutras of Patanjali**
The foundational text of classical yoga: a collection of 196 short aphorisms (sutras) attributed to the sage Patanjali, compiled roughly 2,000 years ago. It defines yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind and lays out the "eight limbs" of practice.

**Eight limbs (ashtanga)**
Patanjali's eightfold path. It begins with the yamas (ethical restraints) and niyamas (observances), moves through asana (posture), pranayama (breath control), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration), and dhyana (meditation), and culminates in samadhi, a state of absorbed meditative union.

**Bhakti, karma, and jnana yoga**
The three classical paths to moksha (liberation), set out in the Bhagavad Gita. Bhakti yoga is the path of loving devotion to a personal deity (central to Vaishnavism and Shaivism), karma yoga is the path of selfless action, and jnana yoga is the path of knowledge or wisdom.

**Hatha yoga and asanas**
The physical branch of yoga, built on asanas (bodily postures) such as Cobra, Camel, and Downward Dog, together with breathing techniques. It is the basis of most yoga practiced as exercise in the West.

**Swami Vivekananda and Raja Yoga**
The Indian monk who introduced yoga and Vedanta to the West, most famously at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. His 1896 book Raja Yoga translated and commented on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. "Raja" ("royal") yoga has become a common name for Patanjali's meditative system.

**Pranayama**
Regulated breathing exercises, one of the eight limbs, meant to control and extend prana, the vital life force that flows through the body.

**Surya Namaskar (Sun Salutation)**
A flowing sequence of asanas performed as a single routine. It is a staple of modern exercise-oriented yoga, though it is not part of the ancient tradition.

**Samkhya, purusha, and prakriti**
The Yoga school is one of the six orthodox darshanas (schools) of Hindu philosophy and draws on the closely related Samkhya school's dualism. Its goal is to free purusha (pure witness-consciousness) from its entanglement with prakriti (matter or nature).

**Kundalini**
A coiled serpent energy believed to rest at the base of the spine, regarded as a form of the goddess Shakti. Kundalini and laya yoga aim to awaken it, using techniques such as mula bandha (the "root lock," a contraction of the pelvic floor), so that it rises through the body's chakras.

**Tirumalai Krishnamacharya and vinyasa**
The 20th-century Indian teacher often called the father of modern yoga, who revived hatha yoga. He developed vinyasa, a style that links asanas through breath-coordinated movement, and trained influential teachers such as B.K.S. Iyengar and K. Pattabhi Jois.

**Yogacara**
A school of Mahayana Buddhist philosophy founded by the half-brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, whose name means "practice of yoga." It taught that reality is "consciousness-only" and was the main rival of Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka school.

**"Union" and the word "yoke"**
"Yoga" comes from the Sanskrit root yuj, "to join" or "to yoke," and is often interpreted as union with the divine or the universal self. It shares an Indo-European root with the English "yoke," the wooden bar that harnesses oxen.

**Katha Upanishad**
One of the earliest texts to describe yoga. In it, the god of death Yama teaches the boy Nachiketa that yoga, the steady control of the senses, is the path to realizing the atman (the true self).

**Ra Ma Institute and Guru Jagat**
A Kundalini yoga school founded by the teacher Guru Jagat, which drew controversy and accusations of cult-like behavior.
